title: How Poor Things Confused Sex With Freedom
description:
How did Poor Things make a male fantasy look like female freedom? In this video, I break down why Poor Things isn’t the feminist triumph it was celebrated as, and why Bella Baxter’s liberation keeps coming back to sex.

Yorgos Lanthimos’ 2023 film starring Emma Stone won four Oscars, including Best Actress, and was praised as a radical portrait of female freedom. But I think its version of empowerment is shaped by the male gaze. I talk about Bella’s premise and the “Born Sexy Yesterday” trope, Max and Duncan, why the film centers her sexual awakening over everything else, its romanticized take on sex work, how Harry and Toinette exist mainly to educate Bella, the goat-brain ending, and why great production design and awards don’t make a film’s message meaningful. This is a Poor Things review from a Lanthimos fan who really wanted to love it.

Did you think Poor Things was a feminist movie? Let me know in the comments!

Hi, I’m Manika! I’m a Black woman who loves movies, TV, and pop culture, and on this channel I share film commentary, TV analysis, and honest reviews from my perspective. I’m less interested in whether something is “good or bad” and more interested in why it works, why audiences react the way they do, and what it says about culture. If you’re looking for movie commentary and pop culture video essays from a Black woman, you’re in the right place.

I’m posting a new video every day in October (VEDO), so subscribe and come back tomorrow.

segments.text: Poor Things is a 2023 film directed by Yorgosanthamos, written by Tony McNamera, and it is based on Alistair
Gay's 1992 novel. It premiered at the Venice Film Festival where it won the Golden Lion, and it went on to gross
more than 117 million worldwide on a 35 million budget, becoming Lanthamos's highest grossing film. The film was a
major award success. It was named one of the top 10 films of 2023 by the National Board Review and the American Film Institute and won four Academy Awards,
two Golden Globes, and five BAFTAs with Emma Stone winning best actress at each ceremony. Many critics have called this film a feminist story, celebrating
Emma's character, Bella Baxter, as a radical portrait of female freedom.
Other critics have called it a male sexual fantasy and a shallow version of liberation. Now, before I start this video, I do want to say that I am a huge
fan of Yorgosanos. I love so many of his films. I love uh Dog Teeth. I love The
Favorite, The Lobster, The Killing of the Sacred Deer. I've watched a lot of his movies. And one thing I do love about his films is that they're very
different. They're very unique. I think he has a very unique way of, you know, telling a very challenging story. And
keeping all that in mind, I was not a fan of Poor Things. I really wanted to go see it because once again, I love Yogurt Smith the most and I also love
Emma Stone, but this movie is not for me. Poor Things is a film centered on a woman with a mind of a child who does mature and grow up throughout the film,
but it's clear that most of the men that she interacts with only want to be with her because of her innocence and assumed
naive. It makes her sexuality the main key to her personal liberation. And although the film has received many
accolades and awards, that doesn't mean that it's good. The film is set in retrofuturistic Victorian London.
Medical student Max Mcandles played by Rama Yusef is recruited by the eccentric scientist Godwin Baxter played by William Defoe to observe a strange young
woman in his home. Godwin reveals that her body belonged to a pregnant woman who took her own life by jumping from a bridge and he replaced her brain with her unborn child's brain. Imagine that.
Taking the body of a woman and giving her a baby brain. Meet Bella Baxter, played by Emma Stone. Bella begins to learn and absorb things very quickly.
She learns how to speak. She's curious.
She's hungry for independence and knowledge. Bella is a character who's not held back by shame. and she doesn't have a strong grasp on social cues,
which lends to the comedic aspect of the film. So, as you watch the movie, you will see that most of the men Bella interacts with, like I said before, a lot of them claim to be in love with
her. First, there's Max, who proposes to her while her brain is still undercooked, so to speak. And then there's Duncan Wetburn, who is played by
Mark Ruffalo, who seduces her and whisks her away from her father's home. So, it is obvious that these men are interested in Bella because at this stage in her
life, she is still naive. She's still very young. her braids have fully developed. And this is literally the born sexy yesterday trope. A woman in an
adult body, but she has childlike understanding becomes an object of desire due to her innocence. The men in
this film fawn over Bella and try to take advantage of her. And I understand that their attraction to Bella is the very thing the film critiques and satarizes, but it doesn't help that we
don't truly learn more about Bella outside of her sexuality. Her first tastes of freedom are sexual in nature.
She pleasures herself early in the film and that somehow leads to her mind maturing. So we see the film links her early growth and development to sexual
discovery. And I think it gives us the wrong impression that women who are more sexually active are more mature or wiser. So moving on, Bella goes to
Lisbon with Duncan and they spend most of their time having sex. As Bella gains more intelligence, she no longer follows Duncan around like a lost puppy. So in
turn, he becomes resentful and desperate. And it is clear that as Bella gains more independence and she gains more intelligence, she doesn't want to
be around Duncan as much. She's less dependent on him. Later in the film, they are stuck in Paris with no money. So, Bella goes to work in a brothel.
This is where I start to really dislike the movie. And I will say that there's nothing wrong with sex or finding confidence or liberation in sexual
pleasure, but the film centers most of Bella's development around her growing sexual experience. Bella is well read.
She questions things around her. She soaks up information like a sponge. But the film spends so much time and so much energy exploring her sexual freedom more
than anything else. This idea that women can feel liberated if they have more sex, is so benol and limited. It clearly
fits into this male fantasy. Bella, although smart and curious, becomes a sexual object for the male gays. I love that she took the initiative to find a
job that will help her earn more money on her own terms. But that's not even how sex work really works. I understand that this film is based on a book set in
the 1800s. However, things could be changed for a modern audience. In the movie, Bella chooses who she wants to sleep with. And for some sex workers,
they don't have that option. She makes it seem like it's such an eye-opening experience to earn money, but many women in sex work can find it to be mundane
doing this thing over and over and over again. They don't find it like exciting or like sexually pleasing. They see it as work. and sex work is not always as
interesting and sexy as the film depicts. She treats it as this curious discovery of the male physique and her own understanding of her own sexuality
and what pleases her. And that's great, but I think this is a more romanticized and idealized version of what it means to be a sex worker. And of course, men
would think, oh, a woman can lay on her back and get $1,000 so easily just by having sex, which is also not how sex works.
And I want to stress that it is great that Bella feels like she's in control of her life now. And I know that the film is satarizing male possessiveness,
male insecurity, things like that. But I will say that I find it odd how much emphasis is put on her sexual freedom.
Like that's the most important thing for her to feel liberated. I like that Bella learns about philosophy and socialism and income inequality, but she doesn't pursue more knowledge on that subject.
And I would like to point out that yes, Bella reads on the ship um when Duncan takes her to the cruise ship and she
debates a philosophy with the character Harry Ashley, but those are small instances of her looking to expand her mind. Most of the film is centered
around her sexual activity. And you could show a woman who's liberated, but why does she only feel liberated when she's having sex? So, let's go back to
Harry Ashley, who I just mentioned. On the cruise ship, Bella befriends Harry and he is played by Gerard Carmichael, a
cynic who shows her how the other side lives. When the ship docks in Alexandria, Bella is shocked by the amount of poor people she sees. Due to
her guilt, she takes Duncan's money to some crew members, asking if they can give it to the poor. At the brothel, she becomes friends with Twinette, who is
played by Susie Ba, and Twinette teaches her about socialism. Now, as a big fan of Yorgosanthamos, I can confidently say
that he doesn't have a lot of diversity in his films. That being said, I was very excited to see Gerard Carmichael was cast in this movie, but I was very
disappointed with his with how much he contributed to the film. I will say I think that diversity is so important and it's great to include a cast of

characters who don't look the same in your movies. However, if you're going to cast black people in your films, you need to be mindful of how you present these characters. The only two black people in this film serve as educators.
Harry teaches Bella about income inequality, philosophy, and opens her eyes to see that the world is not fair.
Twinette teaches her about socialism, politics, and freedom. We learn nothing about these characters outside of their service to the main character. Harry and
Twinette are only in the film to help guide young Bella so she can understand the world in a deeper way, and that's it. It follows a pattern of black characters existing to enlighten the
white character, to guide them, to advise them, help them, and then they fade into the background. And I also want to add that I love that Bella is so
curious about things. I'm glad that she has her own sense of self and knowledge that she develops as she experiences more things. Even when she's talking to Harry, she has her own point of view.
She doesn't take everything he says and believes it to be true. She forms her own opinion. And that's great. But I would have liked to have seen her pursue
knowledge more. I would have liked to see her go to a museum, do literally anything else to feed herself intellectually. It seems like the only
things she sees worth pursuing in terms of knowledge or gaining more experience about is sex because we see her reading on the cruise ship maybe like once and
I've seen her have sex in this movie like 20 times. I know that the film is based on a book but there could have been liberties taken to expand upon
Bella's character more deeply more richly to flesh it out a little bit more to make her character more full-fledged as someone who's has more interest in
pursuing freedom through her sexual desire. In the final act of the film, Bella returns to London to marry Max, but the wedding is interrupted by Duncan and General Alfie Blessington.
Blessington claims that Bella is his wife and she realizes that she took her own life to escape him. So, Bella agrees to go with Blessington and the reason why she agreed to deal with him is
because she wanted to learn more about her previous life and she discovers why she left because he confines her to the mansion. He threatens her with genital
mutilation and forced pregnancy. He holds her at gunpoint and basically they start fighting and then he shoots himself in the foot. So Bella returns to
Godwin's estate and has Max help her put a goat brain in blessed his head. So the film ends with Bella studying for
medical exams and she's in the garden with Max and Twinette enjoying and excited for her new life. And the film ends with Bella becoming someone who
desires to pursue a science as she started her journey as someone who is controlled by it. Poor Things shows the
limited imagination men have about women's interior lives. In my opinion, I think that men assume that a woman with
no shame is a woman who is sexually available because for them, if they were unburdened by sexual rules, then they would try to have more sex. Men feel
powerful when they're having sex or when they're the object of someone's desire.
And it reminds me of a video I saw once where someone asked women on the street, "What would you do if there's no crime?" or what would you do if you were guaranteed 100% safety at night? And
most of the women said, "Oh, I would go for a walk. I would go to the bar and get drinks. I would travel." And when men were asked the same question, they couldn't think of an answer because they
don't have to be cognizant of their safety. They don't feel unsafe at night in the same way that women feel unsafe at night. And also reminds me of something that I saw another courier
talk about on Tik Tok. How he went to different cities around the US and saw couples and groups of women out having fun gathering at restaurants enjoying
their time. But he didn't see groups of men out doing the same thing. It seems like many men nowadays lack the imagination to seek relationships out of

gaining something from it. Every day I see more and more evidence that a lot of men don't want to be friends with women unless there's going to be a relationship, unless they're going to get something out of it, so to speak.
They don't desire to go out unless they have to go out. In the same way with poor things, a lot of men don't understand that if given the choice to feel liberated and free, having sex 10
times a day wouldn't be a woman's first choice. Sexuality is an important part of anyone's life who experiences sexual pleasure. And there are women who like
to have sex, but to have that be the focal point in the film about female liberation is so unimaginative.
Liberation could come from companionship, intellect, faith, hard work, so many different experiences.
Although Poor Things does touch on those aspects of life, the focus of Bella's maturing in the film is centered around her sexual awakening. And I will say
that the film is beautiful. The craftsmanship, the production design, costumes, makeup, all of it is very impressive. I absolutely loved watching
this movie in the theater for the first time and seeing how it went from black and white to vivid color. Also, Emma Stone is incredible in this movie, but
then again, she's just incredible in everything she does, so that's not a big surprise. And she's a big reason why I want to watch the movie in the first place, like I said before. And even with
all of those great things in mind, the movie is narratively underwhelming. If I'm being real, I don't really care
about awards that much when it comes to like films that I watch. You know, this film winning all those awards doesn't mean that it was a good film. I
understand that there are some people who love this film and think that it's incredible. It's just that I don't I think that the film's version of female
empowerment is heavily influenced by the male gays. It doesn't truly focus on Bella and her needs and desires. I love seeing her be curious, but I rather her be curious for something outside of sex.
She is clearly smart and strongspirited with a hunger for independence and adventure. Being in Paris with no money was the perfect way for her to take her
life by the horns, to embrace the unknown of what's next and truly be free. And the first thing she does is go to work in a brothel. She can do
whatever she wants and have no shame about it. And she decides to be a sex worker. Be serious. So, in conclusion,
Poor Things is a visually stunning film with a lackluster message about female liberation. A film written and directed by men based on a novel written by a
man. The film fails to escape the limited view of empowerment it's presented to the audience.
